L57: Zotero is an open-source project committed to providing the best tool for managing your research. Our philosophy is that what you put into Zotero is yours, and one of our founding principles is to make sure you remain in control of your data and can share it how you like — or choose not to share it at all.
L58: We are an independent, nonprofit organization and have no financial interest in your private information. We fund further development by offering additional online storage space to people who find the software useful, not by selling data.
L59: ## Data We Collectcite46†# L60: 
L61: Zotero is designed as a local program that saves data to your own computer by default, and it doesn’t require sharing any data with us to be usable. However, some of Zotero’s advanced features require you to supply us with information.
L62:   * We collect the information you voluntarily provide (e.g., your name and email address) if you create a Zotero account and use optional Zotero services. Zotero can be used without creating an account.
L63:   * We collect the library data you upload if you choose to synchronize your library with the Zotero servers. Syncing is entirely optional and is disabled by default.
L64:   * We collect the attachment files you upload if you choose to use Zotero file syncing. File syncing is optional, and you can choose to sync files in your personal library using a WebDAV server instead.
L65:   * We keep a record of the most recent IP addresses used to access your synchronized library in order to let you verify the security of your account and allow you to cite47†revoke access in your Zotero settings.
L66:   * We log visits to our website, including IP address and browser, in order to prevent abuse and to diagnose technical issues. We retain these access logs for 90 days.
L67:   * We log requests made to our servers by Zotero or third-party software, including IP address and client information, in order to prevent abuse, diagnose technical issues, and assess usage. We retain these logs for up to 90 days. You can cite48†opt out of all requests to our servers.
L68:   * We collect error reports that you submit. See cite49†Support Interactions .
L69:   * If you attempt to save something to Zotero and the save fails, we collect information about the failure, including the URL, browser, and version information, so that we can more quickly fix site compatibility issues. We store this information for up to one week. No additional personally identifying information (e.g., username or IP address) is stored, and reports are generally only viewed in aggregate. This error reporting can be disabled in the Zotero and Zotero Connector preferences.
L70: ## Library Statisticscite50†# L71: 
L72: Zotero anonymizes and aggregates synchronized user and group library data to generate statistics on readership. This anonymized and aggregated data only includes publicly available metadata (e.g., publication title and author). This data is never sold or made available in any forms other than ones offered publicly. We may also use this anonymized and aggregated user information for auditing, research, and analysis to operate and improve Zotero services.
L73: ## Security of Stored Datacite51†# L74: 
L75: See cite52†Security of Zotero Data .
L76: ## Disabling Automatic Requestscite48†# L77: 
L78: You can disable all automatic communication with Zotero servers from the Zotero and Zotero Connector preferences:
L79:   * Syncing: Sync preferences → leave unconfigured or disable automatic syncing
L80:   * Automatic PDF metadata retrieval: General preferences → disable “Automatically retrieve metadata for PDFs”
L81:     * We do not log any information about the contents of PDF metadata requests.
L82:   * Open-access PDF retrieval: General preferences → disable “Automatically attach associated PDFs and other files when saving items”
L83:     * If a PDF can’t be saved for an item with a DOI, Zotero will send the DOI to Zotero servers to check for open-access versions. We do not log the contents of these requests. Disabling this preference will disable all automatic attachment saving.
L84:   * Broken site translator reporting: disable “Report broken site translators” in the Advanced pane of Zotero and the Zotero Connector
L85:   * Translator/style update checking: Advanced preferences → disable “Automatically check for updated translators and styles”
L86:   * Zotero update checking: Advanced preferences → Config Editor → set `app.update.auto` to false
L87:     * Automatic update checking is strongly recommended for security and stability reasons.
L88:   * Retracted item checking: Advanced preferences → Config Editor → set `retractions.enabled` to false
L89:     * Retraction checks are performed cite53†without sharing the items you have in your database.
L90:   * Proxy authentication checking: Advanced → Config Editor → set `extensions.zotero.triggerProxyAuthentication` to false.
L91:     * At Zotero startup, HEAD requests are made to a test file on Amazon S3 and selected publisher websites (controlled by `extensions.zotero.proxyAuthenticationURLs`) to trigger a proxy authentication prompt if and only if Zotero detects that a proxy is required to connect to the internet. If you disable this option and require an authenticated proxy, Zotero network connections will fail.
L92: If automatic syncing or automatic translator/style updates are enabled, Zotero will maintain a persistent connection to Zotero servers when it is open in order to provide immediate updates. You can disable this connection by disabling both of those options or by setting `extensions.zotero.streaming.enabled` to false in the Config Editor.
L93: If you use the Zotero Connector without having Zotero open, the Connector will make a daily request to Zotero servers for information on available site translators. It will then download translators for the sites you visit. For example, if you load a New York Times article, the Connector will download Zotero’s New York Times translator and cache it. If Zotero doesn’t have a translator for a specific site, no request will be made.
L94: No information on the specific pages you visit is transmitted, and subsequent requests won’t be made for the same translator until you restart your browser or the translator is updated. You can avoid these requests by keeping Zotero open while you browse the web.
L95: ## Permissions Warningscite54†# L96: 
L97: When using third-party platforms, we request the most restrictive permissions available that still allow Zotero to perform its advertised functions. In some cases, the necessary permissions can sound a bit scary, so we want to explain why they’re necessary.
L98: ### Zotero Connectorcite55†# L99: When installing the Zotero Connector, your browser will warn you that the extension can “Read your browsing history”, “Access your data for all websites”, or similar. These different wordings all mean the same thing: that Zotero can interact with each page as you browse the web. This is the standard permission that browser extensions that run on all pages require.
L100: Zotero uses it to determine what content it can save on a given page and update the save button accordingly, to fetch metadata and other resources that are served from outside of the domain being saved from, and to provide advanced features such as automatic proxy redirection. Zotero in no way reads your previous browsing history, and no data about your browsing activity is stored except when you choose to save a page to either your local or online Zotero library.
L101: The Zotero Connector also requires permission to “Block content on any page”, which is the technical mechanism it uses to enable saving of CSL files to the Zotero app and to show CAPTCHAs when saving PDFs on some websites. No content is being blocked.
L102: ### Google Docs Integrationcite56†# L103: When you first use Google Docs integration, Google will ask you to grant Zotero Google Docs Integration permission to “See, edit, create, and delete all your Google Docs documents”. The plugin requires this permission to insert citations into your documents. The plugin doesn’t do anything else with your document content and doesn’t access documents other than the ones on which it’s triggered.
L104: The integration works entirely locally on your computer, so even when you trigger the plugin on a given document, nothing is sent to Zotero servers.
L105: ## Storage Purchasescite57†# L106: 
L107: We send two pieces of personal data to our payment processor at the time of purchase:
L108: 
L109:   * your Zotero username, in order to associate your payment with your Zotero account
L110:   * your email address, so that the payment processor can send you a payment receipt
L111: We do not collect or store your credit card, banking, or other payment information. When you enter your full name, billing address, and account numbers to complete a purchase, this information passes directly to our payment processor. We never have access to payment account numbers. We send your name and address to our tax service provider in order to calculate applicable taxes for the sale and record the transaction for tax remittance.
L112: ## Support Interactionscite49†# L113: 
L114: Most Zotero support occurs in the public Zotero Forums. If you would like to remove forum posts you have made, you may clear them yourself at any time, though we encourage you to leave your posts up for the benefit of others. If you’d prefer your forum posts to appear under a different name, you can change your forums username from your account settings.
L115: You may be asked to submit an error report or debug output to help us troubleshoot problems. These reports contain technical information about your computer, such as your operating system and installed browser extensions, and may include incidental personal information such as URLs of sites you visited before or while generating the report. You can review the output of these reports before submitting them.
L116: We don’t store any personal information (username, IP address) that links the report to you, and we generally don’t look at reports unless they are referenced by a Report ID or Debug ID in the Zotero Forums. Reports are stored for up to one year.
L117: If you email us, we collect your email address and any other information you provide, and we may store your messages indefinitely to provide context for any future support requests you make.
L118: ## Third-Party Services Usedcite58†# L119:   * All Zotero server data is stored in the United States in Amazon Web Services. See cite52†Security of Zotero Data for more information.
L120:   * Certain operations you perform in Zotero may trigger requests to public third-party services such as Crossref or the Library of Congress for metadata retrieval. These third parties may log your IP address and search terms (e.g., DOI or ISBN) according to their privacy policies, but no other identifying information is provided.
L121:   * When you save items to or update items in Zotero, Zotero may, depending on your settings, connect to the associated sites to download metadata or save PDFs or snapshots. This is equivalent to loading those sites in your browser, and similar privacy implications apply. See cite59†Zotero and Firewalls for access requirements.
L122:   * When using Premium voices with Read Aloud, document text is sent to external providers for text-to-speech processing. Currently, these providers may include Inworld AI or Google. No additional information beyond the document text is sent to the third-party providers. Standard Read Aloud voices are processed entirely on Zotero servers.
L123:   * Some fonts on Zotero’s websites are licensed from myfonts.com. In order to verify Zotero’s compliance with this license, myfonts.com collects your IP address and the URL of the accessed Zotero webpage.
L124:   * When an account is registered, we use Google reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, or Cloudflare Turnstile to verify that it is not an automated registration attempt. We also do this for login attempts.
L125:   * Payment processing is provided by cite60†Stripe†stripe.com .
L126:   * For institutional storage purchases, invoices and payments may be processed by cite61†Intuit†www.intuit.com .
L127:   * Tax calculation, processing, and remittance services are provided by cite62†Anrok†www.anrok.com and cite63†VAT IT†vatit.com .
L128: ## Deleting Your Datacite64†# L129: 
L130: You may delete your Zotero account to remove information you voluntarily provided when you registered to use Zotero services and to remove the library data you provided if you chose to synchronize your library with Zotero servers. To delete your account, visit your cite65†Zotero settings and click “Permanently Delete Account”.
L131: ## Backed-up Datacite66†# L132: 
L133: We make regular automated backups of data on our servers to protect against accidental loss of user data. These backups are intended for disaster recovery and would be accessed only in the event of significant data loss. Backups may be retained for up to 6 months.
L134: 
L135: ## Legally Compelled Disclosurecite67†# L136: 
L137: We may be legally required to comply with requests for data from law enforcement or government agencies.
L138: ## Changescite68†# L139: 
L140: We may update our privacy policies over time. Up-to-date information, including details of new features, will always be available from this page.
L141: ## Questionscite69†# L142: 
L143: If you have any questions or concerns regarding Zotero’s privacy policies, please ask us in the cite3†Zotero Forums†forums.zotero.org or email AUTHORIZED_PROVIDER_INSTANCE.

L6: 
L7: {% hint style="info" %}
L8: Some videos to help you start using JabRef:
L9: * [Intro to JabRef](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11qMBE_PSBw) by JoshTheEngineer (youtube - English - 22 minutes - January 2021)
L10: * [JabRef for beginners (Part 1): JabRef interface and creating a library](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oF22xJ9lDVk) by James Azam (youtube - English - 14 minutes - April 2021)
L11: * [JabRef for beginners (Part 2): How to manage and cite references in MS Word and LaTeX](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q62nO-KDDZw) by James Azam (youtube - English - 11 minutes - April 2021)
L12:   {% endhint %}
L13: ## Main Window of JabRef
L14: 
L15: Upon the first start of JabRef, the main user interface appears. The main elements are:
L16: * Menu bar
L17: * Icon bar (shortcuts for most frequently used features)
L18: * Side bar (for groups and web search)
L19: * The Welcome Tab provides quick actions, common settings, and access to helpful walkthroughs.
L20:   * Quick settings allow you conveniently specify the [main file directory](https://docs.jabref.org/finding-sorting-and-cleaning-entries/filelinks#directories-for-files), change [themes](https://docs.jabref.org/advanced/custom-themes), enable [large library optimizations](https://docs.jabref.org/faq#q-i-have-a-huge-library.-what-can-i-do-to-mitigate-performance-issues), configure the [entry table](https://docs.jabref.org/advanced/main-window), adjust [online services](https://docs.jabref.org/collect/import-using-online-bibliographic-database), and set up [push to applications](https://docs.jabref.org/cite/pushtoapplications).
L21:   * The walkthroughs are designed to help you learn and discover JabRef's features, such as changing preferences, searching libraries, linking external files, and organizing entries into groups.
L22: ![Screenshot of main window](https://2944476579-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2F-Lr3JU9j9iSUW8RYz1hD-2910905616%2Fuploads%2Fgit-blob-a4d7289dd0e96133e95772d93ccc9b5abe7079da%2Fgetting-started-main-screen%20\(1\)%20\(1\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\).png?alt=media)
L23: ## Creation of a new library
L24: 
L25: A "library" is the main file that saves all the information about your collection of references. The storage format of the file is text-based in the BibTeX standard (by default).
L26: 
L27: {% hint style="info" %}
L28: The usage of a text-based file format has some advantages:
L29: * The file is "human readable" and editable with every text editor
L30: * the text format allows for an easy tracking of changes with every common version control protocol (e.g., git)
L31: * and finally: the format is dedicated for the usage with LaTeX; so you do not need to convert it to any other format but you can just directly link to your JabRef library
L32:   {% endhint %}
L33: 
L34: To create a new library, just select the "New library" menu item in the "File" menu:
L35: ![Creating a new library](https://2944476579-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2F-Lr3JU9j9iSUW8RYz1hD-2910905616%2Fuploads%2Fgit-blob-c2530ee10cd5870e06c07bebd247a650a670da9d%2Fgetting-started-new-library%20\(1\)%20\(1\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(1\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(4\)%20\(4\)%20\(4\)%20\(4\).png?alt=media)
L36: 
L37: The main screen is now showing an empty "entry table" we will now start to fill with some entries.
L38: ## Adding of a new entry manually
L39: 
L40: To add a new entry select the menu bar entry "Library" -> "New entry", click on the icon in the icon bar, or just hit CTRL-N.
L41: 
L42: This opens a dialog where you can select the type of reference you want to store. By default all entry types defined by the BibTeX format are available:
L43: ![Screenshot of "new entry" dialog](https://2944476579-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2F-Lr3JU9j9iSUW8RYz1hD-2910905616%2Fuploads%2Fgit-blob-a0e27d5d09573aaa7b144edf07db69e5f5e4012f%2Fgetting-started-new-entry%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\)%20\(3\).png?alt=media)
L44: 
L45: For our running example, we will select "Article".
L46: After clicking on the "Article" button, the dialog closes and the so-called "Entry Editor" is opened for the newly created entry:
L47: 
L48: ![Main window now showing the entry editor](https://2944476579-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2F-Lr3JU9j9iSUW8RYz1hD-2910905616%2Fuploads%2Fgit-blob-52222a8e7a7750057c384b2124984b00bb1002bb%2Fgetting-started-entry-editor%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\)%20\(2\).png?alt=media)
L49: The most important information about the reference to be added can now be entered in the "Main" tab. "Author", "Title", "Journal", and "Year" should be self-explanatory - however, a "citationkey", might not be familiar to you. Basically, the idea of the "citationkey" is coming from working with BibTeX, where it is necessary to have a unique identifier for each entry. This allows for referencing within a document you might be creating using the stored information in your library.
L50: Moreover, also within JabRef this "key" is used for example for cross-references to other related entries or to determine file names for full-text references.
L51: The key usually follows a global pattern and can be easily created automatically by clicking on the "generate" button next to the field.
L52: {% hint style="info" %}
L53: The default key pattern is `[auth][year]`, which means that Author information is followed by the year of the publication, resulting in the example in `Turing1950`. However, the key pattern is customizable to your needs. See [Configuration](https://docs.jabref.org/setup) > ["Customize the citation key generator"](https://docs.jabref.org/setup/citationkeypatterns) for more details.
L54: {% endhint %}
L55: After entering some information, you can see on the right side of the entry editor a preview of the bibliographic data:

L56: While Zotero stores all data locally on your computer by default, Zotero’s sync functionality allows you to access your Zotero library on any computer with internet access. Zotero syncing has two parts: data syncing and file syncing.
L57: ## Data Syncingcite45†# L58: 
L59: Data syncing merges library items, notes, links, tags, etc. — everything except attachment files — between your local computer and the Zotero servers, allowing you to work with your data from any computer with Zotero installed and to view your library online on zotero.org. Data syncing is free and unlimited, and it can be used without file syncing.
L60: The first step to syncing your Zotero library is to cite6†create a Zotero account (which is also used for the Zotero Forums). Then, open the Sync pane of the cite32†Zotero preferences and enter your login information in the Data Syncing section.
L61: 
L62: cite46†Image L63: By default, Zotero will sync your local data with the Zotero servers whenever changes are made. To disable automatic syncing, uncheck the “Sync automatically” checkbox in this section. You can sync manually at any time by clicking the “Sync with zotero.org” button on the right-hand side of the Zotero toolbar.
L64: When Zotero syncs, it automatically applies changes in both directions — any changes you make in one place will be applied to all other synced computers. If an item has changed in multiple places in conflicting ways between syncs, you’ll receive a conflict resolution dialog asking which version you’d like to keep. If you find yourself using a new computer, you can simply set up syncing and Zotero will automatically download all data from your online library.
L65: ## File Syncingcite47†# L66: 
L67: Data syncing syncs library items, but doesn’t sync attached files (PDFs, audio and video files, images, etc.). To sync these files, you can cite48†set up file syncing to accompany data syncing, using either Zotero Storage or WebDAV.
L68: ### Zotero Storagecite49†# L69: 
L70: Zotero Storage is the recommended file sync option. It has several advantages over WebDAV syncing, including syncing of files in cite30†group libraries , web-based access to PDFs and other attachments, easier setup, guaranteed compatibility, and improved upload performance for certain files. Each Zotero user is given 300 MB of free Zotero Storage for attached files, with cite50†larger storage plans available for purchase.
L71: See the cite51†Zotero Storage documentation for more information.
L72: ### WebDAVcite52†# L73: 
L74: WebDAV is a standard protocol for transferring files over the web, and it can be used to sync files in your personal library. (Group libraries cannot use WebDAV.) Your employer or research institution may be able to provide WebDAV storage. Otherwise, there are many third-party options, both free and paid (see cite53†WebDAV providers known to work with Zotero ).
L75: Once you have your WebDAV account info, enter the URL provided by the service, your username, and your password in the cite48†Sync preferences tab . Be sure to select ‘http’ or ‘https’ as appropriate — if you’re not sure, try ‘https’ first. After entering the information, click “Verify Server”. If Zotero successfully verifies the WebDAV account, you’re all set to use file syncing via WebDAV.
L76: Zotero file sync should work with any correctly functioning WebDAV server. Zotero developers cannot provide support for third-party WebDAV servers.
L77: ## Syncing In Practicecite54†# L78: 
L79: If Zotero is set to sync automatically, changes will be synced within a few seconds of being made. Otherwise, you can start a manual sync by clicking the sync button on the right-hand side of the Zotero toolbar.
L80: If you enter the same login information into the Sync preferences on multiple computers, Zotero will sync everything transparently. Your attention should only be needed if the same item or file is edited in conflicting ways in two different places before Zotero has a chance to sync them. If that happens, you’ll be presented with a conflict resolution window, where you can decide which changes to accept.
L81: If you sync from only one computer, you can still view your online library at zotero.org from any computer. Should something happen to your computer or should you want to start using Zotero on another computer, simply set up your account info on the new computer. Zotero will pull down your entire library from the server.
L82: ## Alternative Syncing Solutionscite55†# L83: 
L84: If, for whatever reason, you are unable to use Zotero’s syncing features, there are some alternative ways to sync your data, though there are significant risk and limitations depending on the approach that you choose.
L85: 
L86: Storing the Zotero data directory directly in a cloud storage folder is cite56†extremely likely to corrupt your Zotero database and should not be done.
L87: 
L88: If you want to avoid syncing any data to Zotero servers:
L89:   * You can close Zotero, manually copy your entire cite37†Zotero data directory to a synced folder on one computer, and then restore it — again with Zotero closed — on another computer, as if you were performing a cite57†backup and restore of your data.
L90: 
L91: If you want to use Zotero data syncing but use an external service to sync just your Zotero attachment files:
L92: 
L93:   * You can use cite58†linked files , rather than stored copies of files, with only your attachment files in the externally synced folder.
